paragraphs: This checklist is only for self-questioning and does not constitute hiring criteria, an ability score or a safety assessment. This page follows US O*NET-SOC 49-1011.00, First-Line Supervisors of Mechanics, Installers, and Repairers (the fixed index assigns this asset a Chinese title meaning first-line supervisors of machinery installation and repair; the body follows the official occupational scope). First-line equipment repair management roles vary greatly: manufacturing equipment maintenance and inspections; automotive and commercial vehicle repair workshops; HVAC and refrigeration installation and repair; electrical and electronic equipment repair; elevator, lifting equipment and mechanical door maintenance; heavy and construction machinery repair; integrated facility and building maintenance; household appliance and commercial equipment repair; and equipment rental and outsourced services. A role may lead one workshop or production line, or manage multiple sites and outside contractors. Before comparing roles or career paths, check education and experience requirements; required electrical, welding, special equipment and elevated-work qualifications and training; physical and health requirements and work environments, including noise, dust, oil contamination, heat, cold and confined spaces; scheduling, on-call and emergency response arrangements; and responsibility for cost estimates, budgets, suppliers and bids.

Test your fit with a paper-based exercise. Given an entirely fictional equipment maintenance shift assignment covering equipment types, quantities and operating status; inspection, servicing, fault diagnosis or installation tasks; available personnel, tools, spare parts and specialized devices; equipment history, work orders, shutdown windows and deliveries; a sudden breakdown, incorrect disassembly or safety violation; and required scheduling, assignments, repair and safety checks, records and cost estimates, write a pre-shift safety briefing and work allocation, maintenance sequence and quality standards, power disconnection, lockout, confined-space and elevated-work safety points, spare-parts, tool and equipment allocation and missing-part responses, incident handling and escalation paths, and records and reports related to work orders, working hours and costs. Identify decisions that must be made by the equipment or production manager or appropriately qualified personnel.

Signals worth considering: willingness to lead teams long term in workshops, on site and beside equipment; ability to supervise work under safety and maintenance procedures; and willingness to handle assignments, spare parts, costs and records. Signals calling for caution: reluctance to work long term amid oil contamination, noise and confined spaces; difficulty coping with sudden breakdowns, urgent shutdown repairs and on-call pressure; or imagining the job consists only of scheduling maintenance in an office.
This card is a career exploration reference, not a hiring, ability-scoring, safety or compliance conclusion.

First decide whether you want to make equipment maintenance management a long-term career. It requires leading teams in workshops, on production lines and beside on-site equipment; supervising mechanical, electrical and installation work under safety and maintenance procedures; organizing assignments and schedules; and assuming management responsibility for personnel competence, equipment and work safety. Test this through the paper-based exercise and seven-day tasks on this page.

The work of First-Line Supervisors of Mechanics, Installers, and Repairers follows a cycle of pre-shift safety briefing and work assignment; maintenance and installation operations, safety and quality supervision; spare-parts, tools, equipment and contractor management; records, working hours and costs; scheduling, budgets and customer communication; and personnel and training management. Before the shift, check inspection, servicing, fault diagnosis or installation tasks; available personnel, tools, spare parts and specialized devices; equipment history, work orders, shutdown windows and deliveries; and complete a safety briefing. Determine schedules, sequences and assignments based on priorities, equipment quantities and personnel skills, clarifying maintenance sequences, quality standards and responsibilities. Inspect and supervise work areas, inspect tools and equipment, and train employees in safety to prevent, detect and correct unsafe conditions or violations of procedures and safety rules. Interpret specifications, drawings or work orders, make templates and mark reference points. Perform skilled repair or maintenance using hand or power tools, hydraulic presses, shears or welding equipment. Inspect objects, systems or facilities and analyze information to determine installation, servicing or repair needs. During work, monitor workloads and review employee performance, and inspect, test and measure completed work for compliance with standards or repair requirements. Monitor tool and spare-parts inventories, workshop conditions and maintenance, and requisition materials and supplies such as tools, equipment and replacement parts. Calculate estimated and actual costs for materials, labor, outside contractors and other factors; participate in budget preparation and administration, coordinate purchasing and documentation, and monitor departmental spending. Communicate with management, engineering, quality control, customers or union representatives to coordinate activities or resolve grievances; meet vendors or suppliers to discuss repair products; and review, evaluate and accept contractor bids and coordinate completion. Compile operations and personnel records, including working hours, production records, inventory data, repair or maintenance statistics and test results. Develop or implement electronic maintenance programs or computerized information management systems, and design equipment configurations to meet personnel needs. Develop, implement or evaluate maintenance policies and procedures; investigate accidents or injuries and report findings; conduct or arrange training in safety, repair and maintenance techniques, procedures and equipment use; advise employees on work problems and help correct skill deficiencies; and recommend or initiate hiring, promotion, transfer, dismissal or disciplinary actions. Priorities vary substantially by setting: manufacturing emphasizes planned maintenance, inspections and shutdown management; automotive and commercial vehicles emphasize work orders, repeat repairs and customer communication; HVAC and refrigeration emphasize installation, commissioning and seasonal emergencies; electrical and electronic work emphasizes energized and de-energized work safety and fault location; elevators, lifting equipment and mechanical doors emphasize special equipment compliance and annual inspections; heavy and construction machinery emphasize field emergency repairs and spare-parts dispatching; integrated facility and building maintenance emphasizes response times and multidisciplinary coordination; and equipment rental and outsourced services emphasize contracts, bids, costs and customer satisfaction.

US O*NET-SOC 49-1011.00, First-Line Supervisors of Mechanics, Installers, and Repairers: directly supervise and coordinate the activities of mechanics, installers and repairers; may also advise customers on recommended services (excluding team or work leaders).

entries.question: What do First-Line Supervisors of Mechanics, Installers, and Repairers mainly do?

entries.answer: Responsibilities and outputs differ. This occupation is a first-line management role primarily producing crew assignments and schedules, maintenance and installation quality and safety review, and spare-parts, tool and cost management. Industrial machinery mechanics perform specific machinery repair and installation. Automotive service technicians and mechanics, bus and truck mechanics, and diesel equipment technicians perform vehicle repair. Heating, air conditioning and refrigeration mechanics and installers install, commission and repair HVAC and refrigeration equipment. Electricians and electrical and electronic equipment installers and repairers install and repair electrical and electronic equipment. Elevator and escalator installers and repairers and mechanical door repairers maintain special equipment. General maintenance personnel and maintenance and repair workers perform routine integrated facility and site repairs. This occupation excludes roles primarily performing a single specialized repair trade, and equipment, mechanical or electrical engineering design and manufacturing roles.

subject.name: First-Line Supervisors of Mechanics, Installers, and Repairers
subject.summary: Directly supervise and coordinate the activities of mechanics, installers and repairers; may also advise customers on recommended services (excluding team or work leaders). Tasks include inspecting, testing and measuring completed work using hand tools, measuring instruments or similar devices to verify compliance with standards or repair requirements; inspecting and supervising work areas, inspecting tools and equipment, and providing employee safety training to prevent, detect and correct unsafe conditions or violations of procedures and safety rules; interpreting specifications, drawings or work orders, making templates and marking reference points for employees; monitoring employee workloads and reviewing performance; performing skilled repair or maintenance using hand or power tools, hydraulic presses, shears or welding equipment; calculating estimated and actual costs for materials, labor, outside contractors and other factors; monitoring tool and spare-parts inventories and workshop conditions and maintenance to ensure suitable working conditions; requisitioning materials and supplies such as tools, equipment and replacement parts; communicating with management, engineering, quality control, customers, union representatives or others to coordinate work, resolve employee grievances or identify and review resource needs; determining schedules, sequences and assignments by work priorities, equipment quantities and employee skills; inspecting objects, systems or facilities and analyzing information to determine installation, servicing or repair needs; advising employees on work-related problems and helping correct skill deficiencies; recommending or initiating personnel actions such as hiring, promotion, transfer, dismissal or discipline; investigating accidents or injuries and preparing findings reports; conducting or arranging employee training in safety, repair or maintenance techniques, operating procedures or equipment use; developing, implementing or evaluating maintenance policies and procedures; meeting vendors or suppliers to discuss products used in repairs; participating in budget preparation and administration, coordinating purchasing and documentation, and monitoring departmental expenditures; reviewing, evaluating and accepting contractor bids and coordinating completion of the work; compiling operations and personnel records such as work-hour and production records, inventory data, repair or maintenance statistics and test results; developing or implementing electronic maintenance programs or computerized information management systems; and designing equipment configurations to meet personnel needs.
